expert.by: independent reviewer agent, written without seeing the topic

items.item: Latency is a ladder of orders of magnitude, not a table to memorise: register at most 1 cycle, L1d about 3, L2 about 14, main memory about 240 cycles; the ratio between rungs matters and the numbers date quickly.
Cycles must be converted to time using the clock of the machine at hand; write every tier in the same unit (ns) before comparing.
Why the hierarchy exists: fast SRAM is costly, DRAM needs refresh and is slower; caches work because of locality, so a working set that fits a level runs at that level's speed.
Latency and bandwidth are separate axes: sequential access with prefetching hides DRAM latency, dependent random access exposes it; the same tier can look 100x different.

items.item: Sustained bandwidth is not pin bandwidth: use measured steady-state bandwidth, not the datasheet peak, when estimating.

Lower bound by the roofline form: attainable rate = min(peak compute, peak memory bandwidth x operational intensity); for a scan-heavy job the bytes-moved term usually wins, so time >= bytes / slowest-link bandwidth.

items.item: NUMA is observable and controllable on Linux: numa_hit / numa_miss / numa_foreign counters show whether allocations land on the preferred node, and memory policy (bind, preferred, interleave, first-touch default) decides placement.
Page cache and write-back sit between DRAM and disk, so a 'disk' benchmark can really be a DRAM benchmark and a write can return before it is durable.
Cloud block storage is specified in IOPS and MiB/s caps and a latency class, not by the medium (EBS gp3 vs io2 Block Express); local NVMe and network-attached volumes are different tiers.
